written.myAnswer: Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. Hypochlorous acid helps disinfect the water.
Potassium reacts readily with halogens to form ionic potassium halides. Potassium loses one electron to form K⁺, while a halogen gains one electron to form X⁻.
Bromide ions (Br⁻) in sodium bromide are the reducing agent; they are oxidised to bromine.
Iodine molecules are large and have strong intermolecular attractions. Consequently iodine has a relatively high melting point and is solid at room temperature.
Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine (Cl₂ > Br₂). It accepts electrons more readily and can displace bromide ions from solution.

Fluorine is the most reactive halogen and iodine is the least reactive. Down the group atomic size increases, so the attraction for an incoming electron becomes weaker and the tendency to gain an electron decreases.

Alkali metals become more reactive down the group because their outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily. Halogens become less reactive because atomic size increases down the group, weakening the attraction for an incoming electron.

Alkali metals lose one electron to form positive ions and act as reducing agents. Halogens gain one electron to form negative ions and act as oxidising agents. They react together to form ionic metal halides.
Bromine is larger than chlorine, so the H–Br bond is longer and weaker than the H–Cl bond. Less energy is needed to break it, making hydrogen bromide less thermally stable.
